mainTopic: Counting kings' years from ניסן: the ברייתא's cases and רבי יוחנן's source in the פסוקים
overview: This amud continues the ברייתא about counting the years of a king's reign. First the גמרא finishes explaining the ruling about a king who began on כ"ט אדר: ניסן is ראש השנה למלכים, and even one day counts as a full year. It then asks why the next clause, about a king who began on א' ניסן, is needed. The answer is that it covers a king who was chosen in אדר but began ruling only in ניסן. Next comes a new ברייתא with three cases of one king dying and another replacing him, and the גמרא explains what each case comes to teach. Then רבי יוחנן brings a פסוק that links שלמה's reign to יציאת מצרים, showing that kings' years start in ניסן. The גמרא tests this proof: it uses the 'fortieth year' of אהרן's death in אב and of משה's speech in שבט, plus a גזירה שוה. It then shows that אהרן's death came first because סיחון was still alive then, and the פסוק proving this comes on the next amud.

steps.title: What the first ruling teaches: ניסן starts kings' years, and one day counts as a year
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes explaining the ruling it quoted at the end of the previous amud (אמר מר), about a king who began on כ"ט אדר. It states the two lessons that ruling teaches.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us that ניסן is the new year for kings, and that one day in a year counts as a whole year.
steps.whatsHappening: At the end of the previous amud, the גמרא quoted (with אמר מר) the ברייתא's ruling that a king who began on כ"ט אדר is in his second year on א' ניסן. Here it explains the two lessons that ruling teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lesson one: the count of a king's years turns over on א' ניסן, not on תשרי. Lesson two: the single day of אדר that he ruled counts as a full first year. That is why he is already in year two by א' ניסן.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us. This is the formula for the new point a source is making.
The new year for counting kings' reigns
One day in a year is counted as a full year
The month of Nisan, when the kings' year begins

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that one day counts as a year is the foundation for every case that follows next.

phrases.english: It teaches us
that Nisan is the new year for kings,
and one day in a year is considered a year.
phrases.notes: The king ruled only on כ"ט אדר, yet that one day counts as his whole first year.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּנִיסָן רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לִמְלָכִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the explanation of the ברייתא's first clause, which was quoted with אמר מר on the previous amud.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ruling teaches that ניסן begins kings' years and that one day counts as a full year.

steps.title: Why say that a king who starts on א' ניסן waits a full year?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next clause of the ברייתא and asks why it needs to be said at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'But if he began ruling only on א' ניסן, we do not count a year for him until the next ניסן arrives.' Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next line of the same ברייתא and challenges it as too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If ניסן is the new year, a king who starts on א' ניסן is simply at the start of year one. Of course his second year begins only next ניסן. So what new idea is the ברייתא adding?

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! A challenge that a statement teaches nothing new.
We count
He arose, meaning he began to reign

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לֹא עָמַד אֶלָּא בְּאֶחָד בְּנִיסָן,
phrases.english: But if he ascended only on the first of Nisan,
we do not count a year for him
until another Nisan arrives.
It's obvious!
phrases.notes: This is the גמרא's own challenge to the clause it just quoted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first clause of the ברייתא to the second.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's clause about a king who begins on א' ניסן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Once we know ניסן is the new year, this clause seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The case where he was chosen back in אדר
steps.stepSummary: The clause is needed for a king who was chosen in אדר but only started ruling in ניסן.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where they decided on him already in אדר. You might have thought we should count two years for him, so the ברייתא teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the clause to a special case where it is not obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the decision to make him king was made in אדר, we might count that אדר as his first year, making א' ניסן the start of his second. The ברייתא teaches that the count begins only when he actually starts to rule, not when he was chosen.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for a specific case
They decided on him, appointing him in principle
You might have said. This introduces the mistaken assumption being ruled out.
Two years

steps.whatToRemember: A king's years are counted from when he actually begins ruling, not from when he was chosen. One day before ניסן counts as a full year.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where they decided on him already from Adar.
Lest you say,
we should count two years for him,
it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'It's obvious' challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being chosen in אדר might count as ruling in אדר, which would give him two years by ניסן.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only actually ruling counts. He is in his first year until the next ניסן.

steps.title: A new ברייתא: when one king dies and another replaces him
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives three cases of a king dying and a successor taking over, and explains how the year is counted in each.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If he died in אדר and another took his place in אדר, we count the year for both. If he died in ניסן and another took his place in ניסן, we count the year for both. If he died in אדר and another took his place in ניסן, the first year goes to the first king and the second year to the second king.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא with three cases about a change of kings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the death and the takeover happen in the same kings' year, both in אדר or both in ניסן, that one year is credited to both kings. When the old king dies in אדר and the new one starts in ניסן, a new year has begun in between. So the old year belongs to the old king alone, and the new year belongs to the new king.

keyTerms.meaning: The רבנן taught. This introduces a ברייתא.
In his place
To this one and to that one, meaning to both kings
The month of Adar, the last month before ניסן

steps.confusionAlert: In the third case, the new king does not get the old year just because the throne was empty during it. The year before ניסן is fully the old king's, and the new king's count starts in ניסן.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:

phrases.aramaic: מֵת בַּאֲדָר וְעָמַד אַחֵר תַּחְתָּיו בַּאֲדָר —
phrases.english: If he died in Adar and another arose in his place in Adar,
we count the year for this one and for that one.

phrases.aramaic: מֵת בְּנִיסָן וְעָמַד אַחֵר תַּחְתָּיו בְּנִיסָן —
phrases.english: If he died in Nisan and another arose in his place in Nisan,
we count the year for this one and for that one.

phrases.aramaic: מֵת בַּאֲדָר וְעָמַד אַחֵר תַּחְתָּיו בְּנִיסָן —
phrases.english: If he died in Adar and another arose in his place in Nisan,
we count the first year for the first king,
and the second year for the second king.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new source that applies the rules about ניסן and one-day years to a change of kings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the change of kings happens within the same kings' year, the year counts for both. If it crosses ניסן, each year belongs to one king only.

steps.title: Why say that a year shared within אדר counts for both kings?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the first case of the ברייתא and asks why it needs to be stated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'If he died in אדר and another took his place in אדר, we count the year for both.' Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first case of the ברייתא it just quoted and challenges it as obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already learned that one day counts as a year. The new king ruled some days in אדר, and the old king ruled earlier that year. So it seems obvious that each king gets credit for that year.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said. This introduces a line quoted from a ברייתא that was just cited, so it can be discussed.

phrases.english: The Master said:

phrases.aramaic: מֵת בַּאֲדָר וְעָמַד אַחֵר תַּחְתָּיו בַּאֲדָר —
phrases.english: If he died in Adar and another arose in his place in Adar,
we count the year for this one and for that one.
It's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the first case of the ברייתא from step 4 in order to challenge it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first case of the ברייתא, death and takeover both in אדר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since one day counts as a year, both kings obviously get credit for that year.

steps.title: One year can be credited to two kings
steps.stepSummary: The case teaches that a single year may be counted for two different kings.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that we do not count one year for two kings. So the ברייתא teaches us that we do.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what mistake the first case is coming to prevent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We might have thought one year can belong to only one king, so it should go entirely to the old king. The ברייתא teaches that the year may overlap and be counted fully for both kings.

keyTerms.meaning: A year
For two, meaning for two kings
We count

steps.whatToRemember: Within one kings' year, a single year can be credited to both the departing king and the new king. Once ניסן passes between them, each year belongs to one king only.

phrases.english: Lest you say:
we do not count one year for two kings,
it teaches us that we do.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: שַׁתָּא לְבֵי תְרֵי לָא מָנִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'It's obvious' challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Ruling out a mistaken assumption (מהו דתימא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One year cannot be counted for two kings, so it should belong only to the earlier king.
steps.terutzMaskana: One year can be counted for two kings, so the years of their reigns overlap.

steps.title: King dies in ניסן and a successor takes over that same ניסן: isn't the rule obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the second case of the ברייתא, where one king dies in ניסן and the new king starts in that same ניסן, so the year counts for both. It asks why this needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the king died in ניסן and another king took his place in ניסן, we count the year for this one and for that one. Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next case of the ברייתא and asks why it needs to be taught at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The old king reigned a few days of the new year, starting at ניסן, so the year counts for him. The new king also started in that ניסן, so it is his first year too. Since step 6 already taught that one year can count for two kings, this case seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! Why does this need to be said?
Another king took his place
For this one and for that one (both kings)

phrases.aramaic: מֵת בְּנִיסָן וְעָמַד אַחֵר תַּחְתָּיו בְּנִיסָן —
phrases.english: If he died in Nisan and another stood in his place in Nisan,
we count the year for this one and for that one.
It's obvious!
phrases.notes: The גמרא's question: why does the ברייתא need to say this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the second case of the ברייתא after the first case was explained in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second case of the ברייתא (died in ניסן, successor in ניסן).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Step 6 already taught that a year can be counted for two kings, so this case seems to add nothing.

steps.title: One day counts as a year even at the start of the year
steps.stepSummary: Without this case we might think that 'one day counts as a year' only works at the end of a year, not at the beginning. The ברייתא teaches that it works at the beginning too.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: when we say one day in a year counts as a whole year, that is only at the end of the year. But at the beginning of the year we don't say it. So the ברייתא teaches us that we do.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by showing a mistake we might have made without this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule 'one day in the year counts as a year' was used in the first case for a king's last day of Adar, at the end of the year. We might have limited it to the end of a year, because then the king's reign continues into the next year. This case teaches that a few days at the start of ניסן also count as a full year for the old king who died then.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces the mistaken assumption)
One day in a year counts as a full year
It teaches us (the new point)

phrases.english: Lest you say:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אָמְרִינַן יוֹם אֶחָד בַּשָּׁנָה חָשׁוּב שָׁנָה —
phrases.english: When we say that one day in a year counts as a year,
that is at the end of the year.
But at the beginning of the year we do not say so.
So it teaches us (that we do).

steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows a mistaken assumption (הוה אמינא) that the case is needed to reject.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'One day counts as a year' applies only at the end of a year.
steps.terutzMaskana: It applies at the beginning of a year too, so the old king gets the year starting in ניסן.

steps.title: King dies in אדר and a successor starts in ניסן: isn't the rule obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the third case of the ברייתא: the king died in אדר and the new king began in ניסן. The first year goes to the first king and the second year to the second king. The גמרא asks why this needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he died in אדר and another king took his place in ניסן, we count the first year for the first king and the second year for the second king. Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last case of the ברייתא and again asks why it is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The old king died before ניסן, so the old year is his last year. The new king began in ניסן, so the new year is his first year. Each king gets his own year with no overlap, which seems too simple to need saying.

keyTerms.meaning: The first year goes to the first king
The second year goes to the second king

phrases.aramaic: מֵת בַּאֲדָר וְעָמַד אַחֵר תַּחְתָּיו בְּנִיסָן —
phrases.english: If he died in Adar and another stood in his place in Nisan,
we count the first year for the first king
and the second year for the second king.
It's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the third and final case of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The third case of the ברייתא (died in אדר, successor in ניסן).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each king simply gets his own year, so there seems to be nothing new to learn.

steps.title: A king's son appointed in אדר still counts only from ניסן
steps.stepSummary: The case is needed where the new king was already appointed in אדר and is the son of the old king. We might think he gets two years by ניסן. The ברייתא teaches that his count starts only from ניסן.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where they appointed him in אדר and he is a king, the son of a king. You might have said we count two years for him. So the ברייתא teaches us that we don't.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing the case to a special situation where we might have made a mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the son was appointed in אדר, we might count his days in אדר as one year and ניסן as a second year. That would be especially tempting because a king's son takes the throne automatically. The ברייתא teaches that he gets only one year, counted from ניסן, when he actually began to reign.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a specific case)
They appointed him / decided on him
A king who is the son of a king
Two years

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with step 6. There one year could count for two different kings. Here the question is whether one new king gets two years, and the answer is no.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where they appointed him from Adar,
and he is a king, son of a king.

phrases.aramaic: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: נִימְנוֹ לֵיהּ תַּרְתֵּין שְׁנִין,
phrases.english: Lest you say: let us count two years for him,
so it teaches us (that we do not).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 9 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case (לא צריכא) to a son appointed in אדר.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because he was appointed in אדר, he should be credited with two years by ניסן.
steps.terutzMaskana: His years are counted only from ניסן, when he actually began to reign.
steps.whatToRemember: All three cases of the ברייתא are now explained. (1) A day in אדר counts as a year, so one year can count for two kings. (2) The same is true for days at the start of ניסן. (3) A successor appointed in אדר still starts counting only from ניסן.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's source: שלמה's reign is linked to יציאת מצרים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן proves from a פסוק in מלכים that kings' years are counted from ניסן. The פסוק places שלמה's reign side by side with יציאת מצרים, which is counted from ניסן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: From where do we know that kings' years are counted only from ניסן? From the פסוק: 'In the 480th year after בני ישראל left מצרים, in the fourth year, in the month of זיו, the second month, of שלמה's reign over ישראל.' The פסוק compares שלמה's reign to יציאת מצרים: just as יציאת מצרים is counted from ניסן, so too שלמה's reign is counted from ניסן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement from רבי יוחנן giving the source in a פסוק for the rule that kings' years start in ניסן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק counts the date by יציאת מצרים and by שלמה's reign in the same sentence, and it calls זיו (אייר) 'the second month.' Putting the two counts together creates a comparison (היקש): both are counted the same way. Since יציאת מצרים happened in ניסן, שלמה's reign is also counted from ניסן.

keyTerms.meaning: From where (do we know)?
Compares / links two things (היקש)
The Exodus from Egypt
The month of Ziv, which is אייר, the second month

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the משנה's rule that ניסן is the new year for kings. The rest of the sugya will test whether it holds up.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
From where do we know regarding kings
that we count for them only from Nisan?

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וַיְהִי בִשְׁמוֹנִים שָׁנָה וְאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה
phrases.english: As it says: 'And it was in the four hundred and eightieth year
after the children of Israel left the land of Egypt,
in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv,
which is the second month,
of Solomon's reign over Israel.'
It compares Solomon's reign to the Exodus from Egypt:
just as the Exodus is counted from Nisan,
so too Solomon's reign is counted from Nisan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the ברייתא's details and starts a new section searching for the source in a פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Kings' years are counted from ניסן, learned by comparing שלמה's reign to יציאת מצרים in מלכים א ו:א.

steps.title: How do we know יציאת מצרים itself is counted from ניסן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's proof: it assumes that years since יציאת מצרים are counted from ניסן, but maybe they are counted from תשרי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And יציאת מצרים itself, how do we know that we count it from ניסן? Maybe we count it from תשרי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the foundation of רבי יוחנן's proof. This sets up the next move, where the גמרא will need to prove that the count from יציאת מצרים starts in ניסן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison works only if the years since יציאת מצרים begin in ניסן. Even though יציאת מצרים happened in ניסן, the yearly count might still roll over at תשרי. If so, the comparison would teach that kings also count from תשרי, and the proof falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: Itself
From where do we know?
Perhaps / maybe
The month of Tishrei

phrases.english: And the Exodus from Egypt itself,
from where do we know that we count it from Nisan?
Perhaps we count it from Tishrei!

steps.triggerLanguage: וִיצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם גּוּפַהּ מְנָלַן דְּמִנִּיסָן מָנִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the hidden assumption in רבי יוחנן's proof.
steps.kashyaTarget: The premise that years since יציאת מצרים are counted from ניסן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the years since יציאת מצרים are counted from תשרי, the comparison would make kings count from תשרי too, so the proof fails.

steps.title: Two פסוקים show the year does not change in תשרי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that years since יציאת מצרים start in תשרי. It points out that both אב (אהרן's death) and the following שבט (משה's speech) are called 'the fortieth year,' so the year did not change in תשרי between them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that! It is written: 'אהרן the כהן went up to הר ההר at God's command and died there, in the fortieth year after the Jews left Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first of the month.' And it is written: 'In the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first of the month, משה spoke…' The פסוק calls אב 'the fortieth year' and also calls שבט 'the fortieth year.' This shows that the new year is not תשרי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 12 by bringing two פסוקים that both say 'the fortieth year,' one about a month before תשרי and one about a month after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Months in the תורה are counted from ניסן, so the fifth month is אב and the eleventh month is שבט. תשרי falls between אב and שבט. If the year changed in תשרי, שבט would already be year 41. Since both months are called year 40, the count since יציאת מצרים must start in ניסן.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't even think that. A strong rejection of a suggestion.
The mountain where אַהֲרֹן died.
Eleven (the eleventh month).
From the fact that it stands at (it is speaking about).
This implies. It marks an inference drawn from the פסוקים.

steps.confusionAlert: 'Fifth month' and 'eleventh month' are counted from ניסן, not from תשרי. Fifth means אב and eleventh means שבט. Without this, the proof makes no sense.
steps.whyThisMatters: This restores רבי יוחנן's proof. If years since יציאת מצרים start in ניסן, then שלמה's years, which the פסוק places side by side with יציאת מצרים, also start in ניסן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 12 that years since יציאת מצרים are counted from תשרי.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Scriptural proof that defends the assumption under attack
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Years since יציאת מצרים might be counted from תשרי, which would break רבי יוחנן's proof.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since אב and the following שבט are both in 'the fortieth year,' the year does not turn over in תשרי. The count since יציאת מצרים is from ניסן.

steps.title: Maybe משה's forty years are counted from the משכן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof. The פסוק about אהרן says outright that it counts from יציאת מצרים, but the פסוק about משה does not. Maybe משה's 'fortieth year' counts from when the משכן was set up.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, the first פסוק clearly says it counts from יציאת מצרים. But this second one, how do we know it counts from יציאת מצרים? Maybe it counts from the setting up of the משכן!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pokes a hole in the proof. Only one of the two פסוקים actually says what the forty years are counted from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof needs both 'fortieth years' to be on the same count. The משכן was set up about a year after יציאת מצרים, in ניסן of the second year. If משה's 'fortieth year' is counted from the משכן, the two dates are on different counts and cannot be compared.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, it makes sense regarding… Used to set up a contrast.
It is stated explicitly.
Perhaps.
The setting up of the Tabernacle.

phrases.english: Granted, that one (אהרן's death)
it is stated explicitly that it counts from the Exodus,
but this one (משה's speech),
from where do we know it counts from the Exodus?
Perhaps it counts from the setting up of the Tabernacle?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא הַיְאךְ מְפָרֵשׁ דְּלִיצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם, אֶלָּא הַאי, מִמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks a hidden assumption of the proof in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that משה's 'fortieth year' (דברים א:ג) is counted from יציאת מצרים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second פסוק never says what it counts from. If it counts from the משכן, the two 'fortieth years' are different years and the proof falls.

steps.title: A גזירה שוה links the two fortieth years
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with a גזירה שוה, using the same method as רב פפא. The matching words 'fortieth year' in both פסוקים teach that both count from יציאת מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב פפא said, 'twentieth year' and 'twentieth year' are linked by a גזירה שוה. Here too, 'fortieth year' and 'fortieth year' are linked by a גזירה שוה. Just as here it counts from יציאת מצרים, so too there it counts from יציאת מצרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא borrows a method רב פפא used elsewhere and applies it here. The same phrase in two פסוקים carries the same meaning in both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא linked two 'twentieth year' פסוקים with a גזירה שוה. That case is discussed later in the sugya. In the same way, the phrase 'fortieth year' in משה's פסוק borrows the clear meaning of 'fortieth year' in אהרן's פסוק. So both are counted from יציאת מצרים, and the comparison holds.

keyTerms.meaning: As (so-and-so) said. It brings in an outside statement.
A teaching that links two פסוקים through a shared word or phrase.
Here too.
Just as here… so too here. The standard formula for applying a comparison.

phrases.english: As Rav Pappa said:

steps.terutzResolutionType: Interpretive link (גזירה שוה) between two פסוקים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: משה's 'fortieth year' might be counted from הקמת המשכן.
steps.terutzMaskana: Through the shared phrase 'fortieth year,' משה's פסוק is also counted from יציאת מצרים.
steps.whyThisMatters: It keeps both dates on one count, which the proof from step 13 needs.

steps.title: Maybe the שבט event came first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a new problem. How do we know אהרן's death in אב came before משה's speech in שבט? If שבט came first, the proof falls apart.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how do we know that the event of אב came first? Maybe the event of שבט came first!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks another hidden assumption in the proof. It assumed the אב event happened before the שבט event.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אב came first, the next שבט is after תשרי, so 'same year' rules out a תשרי new year. But if שבט came first, the next אב is reached by passing ניסן, not תשרי. Then both months could be in year 40 even with a תשרי count, so the proof no longer works.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where (do we know)?
Event, incident.
Came first, preceded.

phrases.english: And from where do we know that the incident of Av came first?
Perhaps the incident of Shevat came first!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 15 secured the shared count, this attacks the order of events assumed in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that אהרן's death in אב came before משה's speech in שבט.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If שבט came first, then no תשרי falls between the two months, and both could be 'year 40' even if years are counted from תשרי.

steps.title: אהרן's death came first because סיחון was still alive then
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that משה's speech in שבט came before אהרן's death in אב. משה spoke after defeating סיחון, and סיחון was still alive when אהרן died. So אהרן's death came first.
steps.simpleTranslation: That can't be! It is written that משה spoke 'after he had struck down סיחון.' And when אהרן died, סיחון was still alive, as it is written: (the proof verse comes next).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 16 and proves that אהרן's death in אב came before משה's speech in שבט. The step ends with 'as it is written,' so the גמרא is setting up a פסוק that will prove סיחון was still alive when אהרן died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה's speech happened after סיחון was defeated, because דברים 1:4 says so. If סיחון was still alive when אהרן died, then the order must be: אהרן dies (אב), then סיחון is defeated, then משה speaks (שבט). That puts the אב before the שבט, so the proof from Step 13 works again.

keyTerms.meaning: It should not enter your mind. A strong rejection of a suggested idea.
After he struck down (defeated).
King of the אמורי, defeated by בני ישראל near the end of the 40 years in the desert.
His soul rested. A polite way to say that someone died.
Still, yet.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the proof is finished in this step. The גמרא has only claimed that סיחון was alive when אהרן died. The פסוק proving it comes in the next lines.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rebuilds the time order the whole proof needs. If the אב came first and the following שבט is still 'the fortieth year,' then the year did not change in תשרי. That supports counting from ניסן.
